problem.statement: A lambda passed to Dispatcher.Invoke captures 'this' (or view-model fields), keeping a strong reference alive that prevents the view model from being disposed or garbage collected, causing a memory leak.

persona.primary: WPF developer maintaining a legacy .NET desktop application

context.situation: A WPF developer maintaining a legacy .NET/WPF app is debugging a memory leak where refreshing a view model from a background thread via Dispatcher.Invoke keeps the view model alive.

current_workarounds: Manually narrowed the leak to a specific refresh method by code inspection

possible_wedges.offer: Roslyn/VS analyzer rule that flags Dispatcher.Invoke/BeginInvoke lambdas capturing 'this' or instance fields, warning of a likely GC-retention leak.
CLI linter for legacy WPF codebases that scans for Dispatcher-closure leak patterns as part of CI, feeding into a broader audit report.
Standalone memory-leak scanner for WPF solutions that highlights view models retained via Dispatcher lambda captures.

risks: Single evidence item (one Stack Overflow-style question), so demand and frequency of this exact pattern are unverified.
Signals show low commercial intent (0.1) and zero commitment (0.0) -- the asker wants a code fix, not a tool or audit service.
No existing substitute tools were mentioned, so it's unclear whether developers would look for/pay for a dedicated detector versus just fixing the one call site.
Unclear if this leak pattern is common enough across legacy WPF codebases to justify a dedicated audit rule versus general leak-detection profiling tools already in use.

cheapest_experiment.hypothesis: WPF developers hitting this specific Dispatcher.Invoke lambda-capture leak would install/use a free static-analysis rule that flags it automatically, and some would want it bundled into a broader legacy WPF audit tool.
cheapest_experiment.input: Publish a single free Roslyn analyzer/diagnostic rule that detects Dispatcher.Invoke/BeginInvoke lambdas capturing 'this' or view-model fields; post it as an answer/tool link on the relevant WPF forum threads and a legacy-.NET subreddit.
cheapest_experiment.output: Install count / GitHub stars on the analyzer repo, plus any comments asking for more rules or an audit report of a whole codebase.
cheapest_experiment.commitment_event: A developer installs the analyzer in their project or explicitly asks to run it against their full WPF codebase.
cheapest_experiment.success_threshold: 10+ installs or explicit 'run this on my codebase' requests within 2 weeks of posting.
cheapest_experiment.failure_threshold: Fewer than 3 installs/requests and no unprompted follow-up questions after 2 weeks.
